papers.title: Context Cache: Efficient Long-Context Inference with Semantic-Aware Prompt Compression
papers.abstract: Long-context language models can process up to 1M tokens, but the quadratic cost of attention makes practical deployment expensive. We introduce Context Cache, a semantic-aware prompt compression system that caches and reuses compressed representations across similar queries. Unlike naive token-level pruning, Context Cache operates at the semantic chunk level: it partitions prompts into coherent segments, computes semantic embeddings, and identifies reusable blocks that appear across multiple queries (e.g., system prompts, shared context, retrieved documents). On a benchmark of multi-turn RAG tasks with shared document sets, Context Cache achieves 2.7x latency reduction and 60% KV-cache memory savings while preserving 97% of task accuracy. The system integrates with vLLM and SGLang serving backends with minimal code changes, making it immediately deployable in production RAG pipelines.

papers.title: AgentSandbox: A Reproducible and Scalable Evaluation Platform for LLM-based Agents
papers.abstract: Evaluating LLM-based agents is challenging due to non-deterministic behavior, external API dependencies, and lack of reproducibility. We present AgentSandbox, an open-source evaluation platform that provides fully deterministic, reproducible environments for agent testing. Key innovations include: (1) hermetic containers that mock all external dependencies (file system, network, APIs) with record-replay capabilities, (2) a protocol for defining evaluation tasks as stateful environments with clear success criteria, and (3) a scoring framework that separates reasoning quality from execution correctness. AgentSandbox ships with 200 evaluation tasks across 5 domains (coding, data analysis, web browsing, system administration, multi-tool orchestration). We benchmark 12 frontier models and find that agent capabilities vary dramatically across domains: GPT-4.1 excels at coding (82% success) but struggles with system administration (34%), while Claude 3.5 shows more balanced performance (68%/61%). All experiments are one-click reproducible.

papers.title: Safety Rigor via Red Teaming Games: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Adversarial LLM Safety Evaluation
papers.abstract: Current LLM safety evaluations treat red teaming as a fixed benchmark, which fails to capture the adversarial and adaptive nature of real-world threats. We formalize LLM safety evaluation as a Red Teaming Game (RTG), a two-player zero-sum game between an attacker and a defender. The attacker generates adversarial prompts to elicit unsafe outputs, while the defender adapts safety training and guardrail configurations. We prove that under mild assumptions, the game has a unique mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium that provides rigorous safety guarantees. Empirically, we instantiate RTG with 12 attack strategies and 8 defense configurations across 6 safety categories. The equilibrium analysis reveals that current production LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0) are significantly more vulnerable than static benchmarks suggest: equilibrium attack success rates are 2.3x higher than the best single-attack baseline. Our framework provides a principled way to benchmark safety under adversarial pressure.

papers.title: Chain-of-Specification: Bridging Natural Language Requirements to Formal Verification with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: We introduce Chain-of-Specification (CoSpec), a framework that uses LLM agents to automatically translate natural language requirements into formal specifications for system verification. The core challenge is bridging the gap between informal human-readable requirements and precise formal languages like TLA+, Alloy, and SMT-LIB. CoSpec employs a multi-agent pipeline: a Parser Agent extracts structured requirements, a Specification Agent generates formal code, and a Verification Agent validates the output against test cases and counterexamples. On a benchmark of 500 real-world system requirements, CoSpec achieves 72% end-to-end translation accuracy, significantly outperforming single-pass prompting (38%) and retrieval-augmented baselines (51%). The framework also identifies ambiguous or contradictory requirements that are common in large-scale system design. We demonstrate practical integration with existing model checking workflows, reducing human specification effort by an estimated 60%.

papers.title: Speculative Retrieval: Overlapping Retrieval and Generation for Low-Latency RAG Systems
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems suffer from latency overhead because retrieval and generation are executed sequentially. We propose Speculative Retrieval, a technique that overlaps retrieval and generation by predicting future information needs based on the current generation context. A lightweight predictor model, trained on retrieval logs, anticipates which documents will be needed for upcoming tokens and pre-fetches them speculatively. When the prediction is correct, retrieval latency is effectively hidden behind generation. On standard RAG benchmarks (NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA, MS MARCO), Speculative Retrieval reduces end-to-end latency by 40-55% with negligible impact on answer quality (less than 1% F1 drop). The predictor achieves 78% top-5 recall for future retrieval needs, and mispredictions are safely handled by falling back to synchronous retrieval. The system is compatible with any embedding-based retriever and transformer-based generator.

papers.title: Adaptive Tool Composition for LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning with Offline Bases
papers.abstract: Tool-augmented LLM agents achieve remarkable performance on complex tasks, but current approaches rely on static tool sets and hand-crafted composition strategies that fail to adapt to novel task distributions. papers.title: MemoryPalace: A Structured Memory Architecture for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
papers.abstract: Embodied agents operating in complex 3D environments over extended time horizons need to maintain and query spatial-temporal memory efficiently. We introduce MemoryPalace, a structured memory architecture inspired by the classical mnemonic technique. Unlike unstructured conversation-based memory, MemoryPalace supports efficient queries like 'where did I last see the red cup?' or 'what changed in the kitchen since I was last here?' in O(log n) time. On the Habitat 2.0 benchmark for long-horizon household tasks, MemoryPalace improves task success rates by 24% over the best baseline (ConceptGraphs) while reducing memory usage by 45%. The architecture is model-agnostic and can wrap any base LLM/VLM planner.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 have shown strong single-chain reasoning capabilities, but they struggle with multi-hop reasoning that requires connecting information across multiple documents or knowledge domains. papers.title: Distilling Reasoning Trace via Knowledge Gap Alignment for Smaller Language Models
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation from large reasoning models to smaller ones often fails because the teacher's reasoning traces contain knowledge gaps that the student cannot bridge. We propose Knowledge Gap Alignment (KGA), a distillation method that identifies and fills these gaps before transferring reasoning traces. KGA first probes the student model on each step of the teacher's reasoning chain to detect comprehension failures, then generates bridging explanations at those points. The augmented traces are used for supervised fine-tuning, followed by a reinforcement learning phase where the student learns to generate its own gap-filling reasoning. Experiments show that KGA-distilled Qwen2.5-7B matches the reasoning quality of Qwen2.5-32B on MATH (93.2% vs 93.8%) and GPQA (71.4% vs 72.1%) while being 4.5x faster at inference. The method is particularly effective for multi-step mathematical and scientific reasoning tasks.

papers.title: GNN-Augmented Retrieval for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
papers.abstract: Standard dense retrieval models treat documents as independent vectors, ignoring the rich structural relationships between entities mentioned across documents. We propose GNN-Retriever, which augments dense retrieval with graph neural networks over a knowledge graph constructed from the document corpus. During indexing, entities are extracted from documents and linked to a global knowledge graph. At query time, the initial dense retrieval results are re-ranked using GNN message passing that propagates relevance signals through the entity graph. On knowledge-intensive benchmarks (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, MultiHop-RAG), GNN-Retriever improves recall@10 by 8-12% over dense retrieval baselines (ColBERT, E5-Mistral) and 5-7% over learning-to-rank approaches. The graph-based re-ranking adds only 15ms latency per query, making it practical for real-time RAG pipelines. Analysis shows the improvement is most pronounced for multi-hop queries requiring cross-document reasoning.

papers.title: BAMI: Training-Free Bias Mitigation in GUI Grounding
papers.abstract: GUI grounding is a critical capability for enabling GUI agents to execute tasks such as clicking and dragging. However, in complex scenarios like the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark, existing models often suffer from suboptimal performance. Utilizing the proposed Masked Prediction Distribution (MPD) attribution method, we identify that the primary sources of errors are twofold: high image resolution (leading to precision bias) and intricate interface elements (resulting in ambiguity bias). To address these challenges, we introduce Bias-Aware Manipulation Inference (BAMI), which incorporates two key manipulations, coarse-to-fine focus and candidate selection, to effectively mitigate these biases. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that BAMI significantly enhances the accuracy of various GUI grounding models in a training-free setting. For instance, applying our method to the TianXi-Action-7B model boosts its accuracy on the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark from 51.9% to 57.8%. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the robustness of the BAMI approach across diverse parameter configurations, highlighting its stability and effectiveness.

papers.title: When No Benchmark Exists: Validating Comparative LLM Safety Scoring Without Ground-Truth Labels
papers.abstract: Many deployments must compare candidate language models for safety before a labeled benchmark exists for the relevant language, sector, or regulatory regime. We formalize this setting as benchmarkless comparative safety scoring and specify the contract under which a scenario-based audit can be interpreted as deployment evidence. Scores are valid only under a fixed scenario pack, rubric, auditor, judge, sampling configuration, and rerun budget. Because no labels are available, we replace ground-truth agreement with an instrumental-validity chain: responsiveness to a controlled safe-versus-abliterated contrast, dominance of target-driven variance over auditor and judge artifacts, and stability across reruns. We instantiate the chain in SimpleAudit, a local-first scoring instrument, and validate it on a Norwegian safety pack. Safe and abliterated targets separate with AUROC values between 0.89 and 1.00, target identity is the dominant variance component (η² ≈ 0.52), and severity profiles stabilize by ten reruns.

papers.title: EMO: Pretraining Mixture of Experts for Emergent Modularity
papers.abstract: Large language models are typically deployed as monolithic systems, requiring the full model even when applications need only a narrow subset of capabilities, e.g., code, math, or domain-specific knowledge. Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) seemingly offer a potential alternative by activating only a subset of experts per input, but in practice, restricting inference to a subset of experts for a given domain leads to severe performance degradation. This limits their practicality in memory-constrained settings, especially as models grow larger and sparser. We introduce EMO, an MoE designed for modularity-the independent use and composition of expert subsets-without requiring human-defined priors. Our key idea is to encourage tokens from similar domains to rely on similar experts. Since tokens within a document often share a domain, EMO restricts them to select experts from a shared pool, while allowing different documents to use different pools. This simple constraint enables coherent expert groupings to emerge during pretraining using document boundaries alone. We pretrain a 1B-active, 14B-total EMO on 1T tokens. As a full model, it matches standard MoE performance. Crucially, it enables selective expert use: retaining only 25% (12.5%) of experts incurs just a 1% (3%) absolute drop, whereas standard MoEs break under the same setting. We further find that expert subsets in EMO specialize at semantic levels (e.g., domains such as math or code), in contrast to the low-level syntactic specialization observed in standard MoEs.

papers.title: Verifier-Backed Hard Problem Generation for Mathematical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities for solving scientific and mathematical problems, yet they struggle to produce valid, challenging, and novel problems - an essential component for advancing LLM training and enabling autonomous scientific research. Existing problem generation approaches either depend on expensive human expert involvement or adopt naive self-play paradigms, which frequently yield invalid problems due to reward hacking. This work introduces VHG, a verifier-enhanced hard problem generation framework built upon three-party self-play. By integrating an independent verifier into the conventional setter-solver duality, our design constrains the setter's reward to be jointly determined by problem validity (evaluated by the verifier) and difficulty (assessed by the solver). papers.title: First-Order Efficiency for Probabilistic Value Estimation via A Statistical Viewpoint
papers.abstract: Probabilistic values, including Shapley values and semivalues, provide a model-agnostic framework to attribute the behavior of a black-box model to data points or features, with a wide range of applications including explainable artificial intelligence and data valuation. papers.title: IConFace: Identity-Structure Asymmetric Conditioning for Unified Reference-Aware Face Restoration
papers.abstract: Blind face restoration is highly ill-posed under severe degradation, where identity-critical details may be missing from the degraded input. Same-identity references reduce this ambiguity, but mismatched pose, expression, illumination, age, makeup, or local facial states can lead to overuse of reference appearance. We propose \textbf{IConFace}, a unified reference-aware and no-reference framework with identity--structure asymmetric conditioning. References are distilled into a norm-weighted global AdaFace identity anchor for image-only modulation, while the degraded image is reinforced as the spatial structure anchor through low-rank residuals and block-wise degraded cross-attention with two-route memory. The resulting single checkpoint exploits references when available and falls back to no-reference restoration when absent, improving identity consistency, fine-detail recovery, and degraded-only restoration quality in a unified model.

papers.title: Static Analysis of Recursive SHACL
papers.abstract: SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language) expresses constraints on RDF data by means of so-called shapes. Its central service is validation: verifying whether a data graph complies with a SHACL document. But so far, there are no static analysis services to compare documents. In this paper, we study the following problem: decide whether all graphs that validate one SHACL document also validate another. Unlike previous works that have considered the implication of shape expressions only, we consider documents comprising (recursive) shape definitions and targets. We show that implication (a.k.a. containment) is undecidable under the supported and the stable model semantics, even for the fragment that uses the description logic ALCIO for shape expressions. Under the well-founded semantics, in surprising contrast, it is decidable in single exponential time. Our key technical contribution is a translation of SHACL under the well-founded semantics into the full hybrid mu-calculus, revealing a novel link between well-founded models and a fixed point modal logic, and a worst-case optimal automata-based decision procedure.

papers.title: A second-order method on the Stiefel manifold via Newton$\unicode{x2013}$Schulz
papers.abstract: Retraction-free approaches offer attractive low-cost alternatives to Riemannian methods on the Stiefel manifold, but they are often first-order, which may limit the efficiency under high-accuracy requirements. To this end, we propose a second-order method landing on the Stiefel manifold without invoking retractions, which is proved to enjoy local quadratic (or superlinear for its inexact variant) convergence. The update consists of the sum of (i) a component tangent to the level set of the constraint-defining function that aims to reduce the objective and (ii) a component normal to the same level set that reduces the infeasibility. Specifically, we construct the normal component via Newton$\unicode{x2013}$Schulz, a fixed-point iteration for orthogonalization. Moreover, we establish a geometric connection between the Newton$\unicode{x2013}$Schulz iteration and Stiefel manifolds, in which Newton$\unicode{x2013}$Schulz moves along the normal space. For the tangent component, we formulate a modified Newton equation that incorporates Newton$\unicode{x2013}$Schulz. Numerical experiments on the orthogonal Procrustes problem, principal component analysis, and real-data independent component analysis illustrate that the proposed method performs better than the existing methods.
